sections.s-hero: Welcome. This course is about the Talent Marketplace, which is how you grow your career at Vanderbilt without leaving it. Maybe you want a bigger role someday. Maybe you're good at things your current job doesn't use. Either way, the marketplace gives you a way to explore, build skills, and be ready when something opens up. It takes about fifteen minutes. We'll cover what the marketplace is, the different ways people use it, how a move actually works, what's expected of managers, and what you can do this week.
sections.s-charge: Quick context before we get into it. Vanderbilt's strategy calls for exceptional core operations, bold new initiatives, and values leadership. All three depend on people, and the university has two ways to get the people it needs: hire from outside, which is slow and expensive, or develop the people already here. The marketplace is that second option. So when you use it to grow, you're not working around the system. This is the system, working the way it's supposed to.
sections.s-what: The marketplace is two things, and it helps to keep them separate. The first is careers of interest. Say you're an analyst and you'd like to move toward project management eventually. You flag it in Oracle, you see what skills the role takes, and you work on the gap over time. When a role opens, staff see it before the public does. Nobody is notified that you flagged anything. The second is short-term projects in other units. If another team needs help and your manager agrees, you can join for a set period, keep your regular job, and come back with new skills and new contacts. One thing to know about privacy: what you explore is yours. Leaders only ever see totals, never names. There's a short true-or-false game on the page if you want to check your understanding.
sections.s-entrances: People come to the marketplace for different reasons, and it's worth figuring out which one is yours. Some people are simply ready for more. The job is fine, they're good at it, and it stopped stretching them a while ago. Some people are good at things their job doesn't ask for. If you were hired as a financial analyst and you've become the person everyone asks for data visualization, your profile is the only place that skill shows up. And some people are in the wrong role but the right place. After a reorg, or when a position is going away, the marketplace helps you find where you fit instead of starting over somewhere else. Whichever one sounds like you, the first step is the same: talk with your manager. Open the doors on the page and read through the one that matches your situation.
sections.s-process: Here's how a move actually works. Most of the time, you're not applying for anything. You're keeping your skills current in Oracle, flagging careers that interest you, and taking learning connected to your goals. That's it, and it's all private. When a role opens that fits, staff see it first. You apply, you interview like anyone else, and if you get it, HR and both managers plan the transition together, usually a few weeks, so your old team isn't left short. The people who land these roles are usually the ones who kept up the everyday part, because they were ready when the posting appeared. There's a short exercise on the page that walks through each step if you want to try it.
sections.s-culture: This section is mostly about managers, but it affects everyone. There's a well-documented problem with internal mobility: managers hold on to their best people. Research puts it at about three in four, and it's usually not malice. It's the pressure of delivering with the team you have. The result is that good people who can't move inside eventually leave. Vanderbilt's rules are direct about this. Managers can't block a move, can't retaliate, and can't see who's exploring. What they're asked to do instead is coach. If someone tells you they're applying for an internal role, the response that works is: thanks for telling me, what interests you about it, and how can I help you get ready. And when someone on your team does move, that counts in your favor. The university kept the person, and you developed them. There's an exercise with five manager responses; try sorting which ones help and which do damage.
sections.s-plan: Here's what to actually do, in order. First, set up a conversation with your manager about your growth. If you're not sure how to open that conversation, there's a short course linked on the card that helps you talk about what you do and where you want to go. Second, use the Talent Marketplace tool to put together a development plan. It maps where you are and what skills your target roles need. To be clear, it's a planning tool; it doesn't guarantee a promotion. Third, fill in your career preferences in Oracle: that you're open to moving, where, and roughly when. Bring that into the manager conversation. Fourth, look through careers of interest. You'll see current openings, career roles, and short-term assignments, and you can flag what interests you privately. Fifth, your skills. Compare what you have, what you're developing, and what your target roles need, then use Learning to close the gaps. Print the job aid; it has all five moves with links. You don't need to do everything today. Book the conversation and you've started.
sections.s-recap: One more thing before the wrap-up: six questions covering what people most often get wrong. What your manager sees when you flag an interest, what a short-term assignment does and doesn't get you, when outside candidates come into the process. After each answer you'll see a short explanation. Worth reading; that's where the details are.
sections.s-close: That's the course. To sum up: the marketplace is where you explore roles, state your preferences, and build skills, privately, with your manager as a partner in it. If you do one thing this week, book the growth conversation with your manager. Everything else builds from there. Thanks for your time.
